Analysis by Richard Cowan 

As regular readers know, I try to keep MarijuanaNews.com “on-topic”, that is on marijuana prohibition. It is certainly a large enough issue with many different facets. (NORML and a few other organizations are chartered specifically to focus on cannabis, and that is a common practice in American politics, where there are numerous “single issue” organizations.) 

When I first began writing about marijuana in 1972, it was almost entirely about “recreational” use, because we were largely ignorant about its medical use, and it would be years before I even heard about “hemp” from some guy named Jack Herer. I can still remember how surprised I was. 

Inevitably, all of the above led to broader questions about the role of the police and prosecutors in our society, and then to questions about how a “free press” in a democracy could fail so badly. That angle became the primary focus of MarijuanaNews.com.

See 

Oh, Joy! New Lies From the Czar’s Little Helper, In The New York Times, Appropriately. 

However, from time to time, it becomes necessary to move beyond the cannabis issues and look at the broader context. Marijuana prohibition does not operate in a vacuum, and sometimes it is impacted by events that have nothing to do with cannabis – or even “drugs.” 9/11 was one example, and the prohibitionists brought the context to us. From December of 2001,

see 

The Endless Cynicism of the Drug Warriors. The Drug War and Terrorism. MarijuanaNews Analysis by Richard Cowan 

Recently, Steve Kubby and I were discussing the problem facing his campaign for the Libertarian Party Presidential nomination created by the perception that his is just a “single issue” candidacy – and it is only about marijuana or medical marijuana. And marijuana is never a “serious issue.” 

See 

Ottawa Citizen Practices First Class Journalism A Brilliantly Insightful Editorial: "Marijuana isn’t just a serious issue. It’s huge."


There is a certain irony to this because marijuana reform advocates have been trying to decouple the cannabis issues from the broader drug war – but the prohibitionist will not let us. Generally, only the Dutch have really done that, and they have not gone all the way.

See 

NORML Sensible Amsterdam Tour A Success. So Is The Coffee Shop System. Seeing Freedom Work. 

Above all else, we have tried to get the sick and dying off the battlefield by carving out an exemption for medical marijuana, but the narks would not even let us do that, and the US is still the only major country where farmers cannot grow hemp. 

See 

Medical Marijuana Endgame: "‘So go ahead and die.’ That would be all right?" "Congress has made that value judgment." Not Really, But The Bush Administration Has. The American People Have Not! 

But if Steve’s campaign broadens its focus to the Drug War in general, which is a very libertarian thing to do, would it still be a “single issue” candidacy? 

No. Let me explain why just the opposite is true. In fact, I think that if any candidate or movement seeks to address any of the other major issues, and yet ignores the Drug War, they will never be able to accomplish their goals. 

A few examples: 

1. In honor of Rudy Giuliani’s late campaign, let’s start with “terrorism” and the government’s misnamed war on same. 

The war in Afghanistan, which we invaded, supposedly to go after Osama bin Laden (remember him?), is going very badly for a number of reasons, but the Drug War is a major part of the problem, because the opium poppy crop is a major source of funding for the Taliban and the other war lords. However, if we try to destroy it, we alienate the poor peasants. 

See 

Cannabis Might Help in Afghan War, But “Words Are, Of Course, The Most Powerful Drug Used By Mankind.” 

Or what about Colombia, where the FARC guerillas are funded by the cocaine trade? Or consider that the Madrid train bombers got their funding by smuggling Moroccan hashish. 

2. Border control, immigration and national security. 

Whatever one thinks about the immigration issue and securing the border – and I mean the Mexican border, because the Canadian border is a joke – the Drug War makes it impossible to get control at the most basic level. 

See 

Data On Mexican Border Seizures Show That Talk About "BC Bud" Is Just More Prohibitionist Propaganda -- But the "Drug War" Is Really Aimed At Marijuana. 

Last December 23, the Houston Chronicle quoted Mike Vigil, the Drug Enforcement Administration's former chief of international operations, as saying, "I don't care if you put 10 Marine divisions along the Mexican border, you are never going to be able to stop the movement of drugs, marijuana, across the border." 

It is obvious that trying to stop it is a huge waste of resources that should be used looking for something that is really dangerous. 

3. Mexico, our third largest trading partner. 

But it gets worse. The Drug War is having a devastating effect on Mexico, inhibiting its economic and political development, driving more and more Mexicans to move north. In 2006, the United States imported $198 billion in goods from Mexico and exported $134 billion to them, making it our third-largest trading partner. It is also a major source of oil. 

See 

New York Times Cheers "MEXICO TO JOIN US IN FIGHT ON DRUGS – Treaty is expected to cut down smuggling across border and break up gangs of dealers." We Couldn’t Make This Up! 

4. Crime. The Drug War is obviously the major source of all crime in the US, other than that committed under the influence of alcohol. Some of the crime is committed by addicts whose chaotic lives make it impossible for them to work, and the prices of contraband are unaffordable except for the wealthy. Other crime is related to turf wars to control the contraband markets. Consequently, we have the world’s largest prison population and spend more on prisons that on higher education in many states. The Drug War is also a major source of one of the most corrosive forms of crime – police corruption. 

See 

Prohibition and The Prison State. “Protecting” Youth and Minorities. In DEAland, The UK and France Prisons Are Full. 

and 

The Drug Testing and Rehab Rackets Keep Prisons Full. From California to the UK The Results Are Tragic – And Expensive. Did Michael Vick Find A Loophole?

5. Public safety and public health. The US has 5% of the world’s population, but 25% of the world’s prisoners. Are Americans really 5 times as lawless as the world average? Prisons are both schools for crime and increasingly a threat to public health as incubators for disease. 

6. Substance abuse: Prohibitionist propaganda undermines credible “drug education”, and its focus on illegal drugs has given rise to the abuse of prescription drugs and alcohol, which are much more dangerous than marijuana. 

See 

Even The Prohibitionists Are Attacking DARE. What Is the Definition of Fraud? Analysis By Richard Cowan 

7. Democracy. After the vote-fraud scandals of the last elections more and more people are waking up to the fact that our democratic system is seriously flawed and in real danger. However, the problems go far beyond the mechanics of vote counting or “campaign finance.” 

Unfortunately, because the Drug War is invisible, no one seems to have noticed that it is perpetuated by the power of the police and prosecutors who control political operations at the most basic level. In a very real sense, the US is already a police state. If that seems hyperbolic, look at Steve Kubby’s story, or the influence of the police when legislatures consider allowing farmers to grow hemp or sick and dying people to grow medical marijuana. 

In the real world of American politics, lawless law enforcement controls the Republican Party and much of the Democratic Party. 

8. Taxes: We are losing huge sums to the black market, even if there are only low sales taxes on marijuana like there is on everything else, and income taxes are paid on the industry’s profits. 

9. The Economy in general: The earning power of people who are arrested on drug charges is significantly reduced in a variety of ways, and they are prevented from becoming as productive as they should be. That hurts the economy, i.e., all of us, not just them and their families. The cumulative effect of this runs into the billions of dollars per year, but I have never seen any econometric analysis of it. 

10. The real estate crisis: Right now everyone is talking about the decline in property values and the adverse effect that has on the middle class. However, the drug war hurts property values in huge areas of America’s cities by making them unsafe. The cost may be in the trillions. 

11. Families: Family Values is one of the most successful slogans of commercial Christianity and its political accomplices, but the Drug War destroys families by locking up mothers and fathers. The number of incarcerated women in the U.S. is up 775 percent since 1977, double the rate of increase for males, which is horrific in itself. Many of these women have children, who then grow up to have difficult lives. 

12. Food and agriculture: Food prices are being driven up by many factors, but one of the major causes is the absurd use of corn for bio-fuels. Hemp would almost certainly be a better source, but the US, the world’s leader in agriculture is not allowed to grow hemp – by the DEA. 

13. The environment: Again, hemp could play a major role in overcoming the effects of deforestation in poor countries like Haiti, but it is not allowed by its American occupiers. Instead, desperate Haitians risk their lives in crowded little boats trying to sneak into the US. (Immigration control?) 

14 Personal freedom and safety: In addition to crime on the streets, we read about police SWAT teams storming the wrong house and killing – or being killed by – an innocent home owner, on almost a daily basis. How many more cases are there that don’t make the news? 

15. Race relations: The legacy of slavery and the racist ideology that was necessary to support it in a country that began with the declaration that “all men are created equal” still haunts our politics, and the racist origins of the Drug War are too well documented to need repeating, but even African American politicians are afraid of the issue.

See 

Obama Flip-Flops On Decrim. Shame on Him, Or Shame on Us? Why Do Politicians Fear Something A Huge Majority Supports? Who Is Their Real Constituency? 

16. And, yes, there is finally medical marijuana. Health care is a major issue in the Presidential campaign, but it cannot really be addressed without considering this quote from the 1999 Institute of Medicine report on medical marijuana: "There is no clear alternative for people suffering from chronic conditions that might be relieved by smoking marijuana, such as pain or AIDS wasting." 

Of course, medical marijuana is even more important than those examples indicate. In fact, people with chronic pain may be the largest cohort amongst medical marijuana users. 

See 

If Being Tortured In Prison Made John McCain a Hero, What About America’s Medical Cannabis Prisoners? And What If They Are His Victims? 

and 

Program Notes for the MarijuanaNews World Report July 11, 2005 Pain Just for the Poor? War On Patients; Allen St. Pierre of NORML On Meth, Marijuana and the Economics of Prohibition. 

But the Drug War also interferes in other aspects of medicine by denying adequate pain relief through better access to opiates. We must put the patients ahead of prohibition. 

Indeed, we must put the country ahead of the Drug War. That is the invisible context of this election.
